about: Sourced life stories for the Pharaohs and the kings of Cush (the Pharaohs of Joseph, the oppression and the Exodus, Solomon's father-in-law, Shishak, So, Tirhakah, Necho and Hophra). Written from Scripture and the reviewed dossier Research/People/rulers-egypt.md.

pharaoh-gen-37-36.short: The unnamed king of Egypt who brought Joseph out of prison to interpret his dreams, set him over all Egypt, and let Jacob's family dwell in Goshen.

paragraphs.text: Genesis never gives this king a name; he is “Pharaoh” or “Pharaoh king of Egypt”. Joseph came to Egypt as a slave, bought by Potiphar, “an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard”. Later Pharaoh was wroth with his chief butler and chief baker and put them in ward in the prison where Joseph was bound. On his birthday he restored the butler and hanged the baker, as Joseph had interpreted.

At the end of two full years Pharaoh dreamed, and none of the magicians or wise men of Egypt could interpret his dreams. The chief butler remembered the young Hebrew in the prison, and Pharaoh sent for Joseph, who told him, “God hath shewed Pharaoh what he is about to do.” Joseph spoke of seven years of plenty and seven of famine, and counselled him to lay up food in the cities against the famine.

Pharaoh asked his servants, “Can we find such a one as this is, a man in whom the Spirit of God is?” He set Joseph over all the land of Egypt, “only in the throne will I be greater than thou”, gave him his ring, fine linen and a gold chain, called him Zaphnath-paaneah, and gave him Asenath the daughter of the priest of On to wife. Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh. When the famine came and the people cried to Pharaoh for bread, he told them, “Go unto Joseph; what he saith to you, do.”

When he heard that Joseph's brethren had come, it pleased Pharaoh well, and he told Joseph to send wagons and bring his father and their households from Canaan: “I will give you the good of the land of Egypt”. He let them dwell in Goshen, “in the best of the land”, and Jacob, a hundred and thirty years old, stood before Pharaoh and blessed him. In the famine Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh, except the priests' land, and made it a law that Pharaoh should have the fifth part.

When the days of mourning for Jacob were past, Joseph asked leave to bury his father in Canaan, and Pharaoh said, “Go up, and bury thy father, according as he made thee swear.” The site's record for this Pharaoh holds Genesis 37 to 50 under one king, but Scripture does not say whether the king who let Joseph bury Jacob was the king who raised him. A psalm looks back on how “the king sent and loosed him”, and Stephen says God gave Joseph favour “in the sight of Pharaoh king of Egypt; and he made him governor over Egypt and all his house”.

pharaoh-exo-1-11.short: The site's record for the unnamed kings of Exodus 1–2: the “new king” who afflicted Israel, the king who ordered the sons killed, and the Pharaoh Moses fled.

paragraphs.text: Exodus begins after Joseph and all his generation had died and Israel had multiplied in Egypt: “Now there arose up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph.” Exodus gives him no name. He told his people that Israel was “more and mightier than we” and might join Egypt's enemies in war. Taskmasters were set over Israel, who built for Pharaoh the treasure cities Pithom and Raamses, and the Egyptians made their lives “bitter with hard bondage”.

The king of Egypt told the Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, to kill every son they delivered. The midwives feared God and saved the boys alive, and when the king called them to account they said the Hebrew women were delivered before the midwives came. Then Pharaoh charged all his people: “Every son that is born ye shall cast into the river”. Stephen, looking back, says that the king who knew not Joseph “evil entreated our fathers, so that they cast out their young children”.

A son born to a man and woman of the house of Levi was hidden three months, then laid in an ark of bulrushes among the flags by the river. The daughter of Pharaoh found him when she came down to wash, had him nursed by his own mother, and took him as her son; she called him Moses. Hebrews says his parents “were not afraid of the king's commandment”.

When Moses was grown he killed an Egyptian who was smiting a Hebrew, and “when Pharaoh heard this thing, he sought to slay Moses”. Moses fled to Midian; Stephen says he was “full forty years old” when he went to visit his brethren. Exodus does not say whether this Pharaoh, the new king of chapter 1 and the king of the midwives were one man; the site's record holds those verses together. In process of time the king of Egypt died, and Israel's cry by reason of the bondage came up to God.

pharaoh-exo-3-10.short: The unnamed king who refused Moses and Aaron through the plagues, sent Israel out after the firstborn died, then pursued them to the sea.

paragraphs.text: From the burning bush God told Moses, “I will send thee unto Pharaoh”. Exodus never names this king. While Moses was in Midian “the king of Egypt died”, and the LORD told Moses that “all the men are dead which sought thy life”. Moses was eighty and Aaron eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh.

Moses and Aaron told him, “Let my people go, that they may hold a feast unto me in the wilderness.” Pharaoh answered, “Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice to let Israel go?” The same day he commanded that the people be given no more straw to make brick, yet make the same tale of bricks, for “they be idle”.

Then came the signs and the plagues: Aaron's rod swallowed the magicians' rods, the river was turned to blood, and frogs, lice, flies, the death of the cattle, boils, hail, locusts and darkness followed. Again and again Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron and promised to let the people go, offering first a sacrifice “in the land”, then the men only, then all but the flocks and herds. Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his heart and that the LORD hardened it. After the hail he said, “I have sinned this time: the LORD is righteous, and I and my people are wicked.”

After the darkness Pharaoh told Moses, “see my face no more”. At midnight the LORD smote all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, “from the firstborn of Pharaoh that sat on his throne”. Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron by night: “Rise up, and get you forth from among my people ... and bless me also.”

When it was told him that the people had fled, Pharaoh and his servants said, “Why have we done this, that we have let Israel go from serving us?” He took six hundred chosen chariots and all the chariots of Egypt, and overtook Israel by the sea. The waters returned and covered “all the host of Pharaoh that came into the sea after them”, and a psalm says the LORD “overthrew Pharaoh and his host in the Red sea”; neither says in so many words that Pharaoh himself died. The LORD's word to him, “for this cause have I raised thee up, for to shew in thee my power”, is quoted by Paul in Romans.

pharaoh-1ki-3-1.short: The unnamed king of Egypt whose daughter Solomon married, and who took Gezer and gave it to her as a present.

paragraphs.text: “Solomon made affinity with Pharaoh king of Egypt, and took Pharaoh's daughter, and brought her into the city of David”, until he had finished building his own house, the house of the LORD and the wall of Jerusalem. Scripture names neither the king nor his daughter. Kings later names “the daughter of Pharaoh” with the “many strange women” Solomon loved.

Pharaoh king of Egypt had gone up and taken Gezer, burnt it with fire and slain the Canaanites who dwelt there, and given the city “for a present unto his daughter, Solomon's wife”; Solomon built Gezer. Solomon also built a house for Pharaoh's daughter, and she came up out of the city of David into it. Chronicles adds his reason: “My wife shall not dwell in the house of David king of Israel, because the places are holy”.

The site's record for this Pharaoh also takes in the Pharaoh of David's day. When Joab struck Edom, Hadad the Edomite fled to Egypt as a little child, and Pharaoh gave him a house, victuals and land, and gave him to wife the sister of Tahpenes the queen; their son Genubath grew up “among the sons of Pharaoh”. When Hadad heard that David and Joab were dead and asked to go home, Pharaoh said, “But what hast thou lacked with me?” Scripture calls both kings only “Pharaoh king of Egypt” and does not say they were one man.

shishak-1ki-11-40.short: Shishak king of Egypt, to whom Jeroboam fled from Solomon, came up against Jerusalem in Rehoboam's fifth year and took the treasures of the temple and the palace.

paragraphs.text: When Solomon sought to kill Jeroboam, Jeroboam “fled into Egypt, unto Shishak king of Egypt, and was in Egypt until the death of Solomon”. After Solomon died, Jeroboam returned out of Egypt. Scripture says nothing of what passed between him and Shishak.

In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem and took away the treasures of the house of the LORD and of the king's house; “he even took away all”, with the shields of gold Solomon had made. Rehoboam made shields of brass in their place.

Chronicles adds more. Shishak came “because they had transgressed against the LORD”, with twelve hundred chariots, sixty thousand horsemen and people without number, “the Lubims, the Sukkiims, and the Ethiopians”, and he took the fenced cities of Judah. The prophet Shemaiah told Rehoboam and the princes gathered at Jerusalem, “Ye have forsaken me, and therefore have I also left you in the hand of Shishak.”

The princes and the king humbled themselves and said, “The LORD is righteous.” The LORD said his wrath would not be poured out on Jerusalem by the hand of Shishak, “Nevertheless they shall be his servants; that they may know my service, and the service of the kingdoms of the countries.” Neither Kings nor Chronicles says that Shishak fought for Jerusalem; both say he came up against it and took its treasures.

so-2ki-17-4.short: So king of Egypt is named once: Hoshea, the last king of Israel, sent messengers to him and stopped his yearly present to Assyria.

paragraphs.text: Scripture names So only once, and says little more. Hoshea king of Israel had become the servant of Shalmaneser king of Assyria and gave him presents. Then he “sent messengers to So king of Egypt, and brought no present to the king of Assyria, as he had done year by year”.

Scripture says nothing of any answer from So. The king of Assyria found conspiracy in Hoshea, shut him up and bound him in prison, besieged Samaria three years, and in Hoshea's ninth year took it and carried Israel away into Assyria. Hosea speaks of Ephraim, “they call to Egypt, they go to Assyria”, but does not name So. Scripture does not say who So was, where he reigned, or for how long.

tirhakah-2ki-19-9.short: Tirhakah king of Ethiopia is named in one report: word that he had come out to fight made Sennacherib send a second message to Hezekiah.

paragraphs.text: Scripture names Tirhakah in a single report, told in both Kings and Isaiah, and calls him “king of Ethiopia”, never Pharaoh. Sennacherib king of Assyria had left Lachish and was warring against Libnah when he heard word of Tirhakah: in Kings, “Behold, he is come out to fight against thee”, and in Isaiah, “He is come forth to make war with thee”.

Hearing it, Sennacherib sent messengers again to Hezekiah king of Judah: “Let not thy God in whom thou trustest deceive thee”. Hezekiah read the letter, went up into the house of the LORD, and spread it before the LORD.

Earlier, Rab-shakeh had mocked Judah's trust in Egypt as “the staff of this bruised reed”, naming no Pharaoh. Scripture does not say that Hezekiah asked Tirhakah for help, or that Tirhakah's army met the Assyrians. That night the angel of the LORD smote the camp of the Assyrians, and Sennacherib returned to Nineveh; Scripture does not tie this to Tirhakah.

neco-2ki-23-29.short: Pharaoh-nechoh king of Egypt killed King Josiah at Megiddo, deposed Jehoahaz, made Jehoiakim king, and saw his army beaten by Nebuchadrezzar at Carchemish.

paragraphs.text: Kings says that in Josiah's days “Pharaoh-nechoh king of Egypt went up against the king of Assyria to the river Euphrates”; Chronicles says he came up “to fight against Carchemish by Euphrates”. Josiah went out against him. Chronicles gives Necho's message to him: “What have I to do with thee, thou king of Judah? I come not against thee this day, but against the house wherewith I have war: for God commanded me to make haste”.

Kings says only that Necho slew Josiah at Megiddo “when he had seen him”, and that his servants carried him dead to Jerusalem. Chronicles says Josiah “hearkened not unto the words of Necho from the mouth of God”, disguised himself and fought in the valley of Megiddo, where archers shot him; he was brought to Jerusalem and died there, and all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for him.

The people made Josiah's son Jehoahaz king, but after three months Pharaoh-nechoh put him in bands at Riblah in the land of Hamath; Chronicles says the king of Egypt “put him down at Jerusalem”. He laid on the land a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold, made Eliakim son of Josiah king, and “turned his name to Jehoiakim”. Jehoahaz was taken to Egypt and died there, and Jehoiakim taxed the people to pay Pharaoh-nechoh. Jeremiah said of Shallum son of Josiah, “which reigned instead of Josiah his father”, that he would die where they had led him captive.

Jeremiah's word against Egypt names “the army of Pharaoh-necho king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates in Carchemish, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon smote in the fourth year of Jehoiakim”. The site's record also places under Necho a cry in the same chapter that does not name him: “Pharaoh king of Egypt is but a noise”. Kings adds, again without a name, that “the king of Egypt came not again any more out of his land”, for the king of Babylon had taken all that was his from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates.

hophra-jer-37-5.short: Pharaoh-hophra king of Egypt is named once, in Jeremiah's sign to the Jews in Egypt: the LORD would give him into the hand of his enemies.

paragraphs.text: Scripture names Pharaoh-hophra only once. Johanan the son of Kareah took the remnant of Judah, with Jeremiah and Baruch, into Egypt, “for they obeyed not the voice of the LORD”, and they came to Tahpanhes. When the Jews in Egypt told Jeremiah they would go on burning incense to the queen of heaven, he gave them a sign: “Behold, I will give Pharaoh-hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies, and into the hand of them that seek his life; as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon”.

The site's record for Hophra also gathers verses that do not name the king. In Zedekiah's reign Pharaoh's army came forth out of Egypt, and the Chaldeans besieging Jerusalem departed for fear of it. Jeremiah told Zedekiah's messengers that the army “shall return to Egypt into their own land”, and that the Chaldeans would come again and burn the city.

Ezekiel, among the captives by the river Chebar, said that the one “of the king's seed” whom the king of Babylon had made king in Jerusalem rebelled by “sending his ambassadors into Egypt, that they might give him horses and much people”, and that Pharaoh with his mighty army would not help him in the war. In the tenth, eleventh and twelfth years he prophesied against “Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lieth in the midst of his rivers”, and said, “I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt”. Ezekiel never names the Pharaoh of these oracles.

At Tahpanhes the LORD told Jeremiah to hide great stones at the entry of “Pharaoh's house”, and to say that Nebuchadrezzar would set his throne on them and smite the land of Egypt. Scripture foretells this, but does not tell how it, or the sign of Hophra, came to pass.
